lesson.title: Where the Watts Go: Power Dissipation in Resistors
lesson.summary: Power dissipation is the rate at which electrical energy converts into heat inside a resistive component, and it can be calculated three equivalent ways depending on which quantities you know.
lesson.body:
Every time current pushes through a resistor, the electrons colliding with the material's atomic lattice lose energy, and that energy leaves the circuit as heat. This process is called power dissipation, and it is the reason resistors get warm, why heat sinks exist, and why a resistor has a power rating printed or implied in its specification just as important as its resistance value. Power dissipation connects two ideas you already know, power itself, the rate at which energy is transferred, and resistance, the opposition that turns organized electrical motion into disorganized thermal motion.

There are three equivalent formulas for the power dissipated by a resistor, and knowing all three matters because different problems hand you different known quantities. The most basic definition is P equals V times I, power equals voltage times current, which works for any circuit element. For a resistor specifically, Ohm's law lets you substitute V equals I times R into that formula to get P equals I squared times R, or substitute I equals V divided by R to get P equals V squared divided by R. All three expressions describe the exact same physical quantity, they simply start from different known information.

Take a resistor of 100 ohms carrying a current of 0.2 amps. Using P equals I squared times R, the power is 0.2 squared, which is 0.04, multiplied by 100 ohms, giving 4 watts. You can check this a different way: first find the voltage across the resistor using Ohm's law, V equals I times R, which is 0.2 amps times 100 ohms, or 20 volts. Then power equals V times I, 20 volts times 0.2 amps, which is also 4 watts. Both routes land on the identical answer because they are the same physics expressed with different algebra.

This is not just a bookkeeping exercise, it has real consequences for component selection. A resistor marketed as a quarter watt resistor is only rated to safely dissipate 0.25 watts continuously, if you push it past that, the excess heat cannot escape fast enough and the resistor's value drifts, its coating discolors, or it fails outright, sometimes dramatically. An engineer choosing a resistor for a circuit has to calculate the expected power dissipation using these formulas and then choose a component rated comfortably above that value, often with a safety margin of two or more.

Power dissipation is also the physical mechanism behind everything from the glow of an incandescent filament to the warmth of a phone charger to the need for fans inside a computer. Anywhere current meets resistance, energy is being converted to heat at a rate you can calculate exactly, and that calculation is one of the most frequently used tools in all of practical circuit design.

It is worth noticing that the two squared forms of the power formula behave very differently as resistance changes, which trips up many beginners. Since P equals I squared times R grows with resistance, while P equals V squared divided by R shrinks as resistance grows, doubling a resistor's value while holding current fixed doubles its dissipated power, but doubling that same resistor's value while holding voltage fixed cuts its dissipated power in half. Knowing which quantity, voltage or current, is actually being held constant in a given problem is essential to picking the correct version of the formula.
